title: Why $15 Today Beats $100 In Ten Years

beats.say: You would likely take fifteen dollars today over one hundred in ten years, and a famous experiment found people do exactly that.
beats.visual: a single worn dollar bill lying on a dark table under a warm lamp, no text

beats.say: The researcher was the economist Richard Thaler, in nineteen eighty one.
beats.visual: an old chalkboard in an empty classroom, no writing, window light

beats.say: He asked how much more money people would need to wait.
beats.visual: a pocket watch swinging on a chain in dim light, close-up

beats.say: To wait one month, the typical answer was twenty dollars.
beats.visual: a calendar page being turned once, hands only, soft light

beats.say: To wait one year, the typical answer was fifty dollars.
beats.visual: a stack of twelve calendar pages on a wooden desk, no text, soft light

beats.say: To wait ten years, the typical answer was one hundred dollars.
beats.visual: a tall hourglass with golden sand running slowly in a dark room

beats.say: So fifteen dollars now felt as good as a hundred dollars a decade away.
beats.visual: a small golden coin glowing on a dark table beside a faint distant stack of coins

beats.say: Here is the part nobody tells you. The brain does not shrink the future evenly. The next few weeks look huge and the far future looks tiny.
beats.visual: a long road narrowing into fog with a bright lamp close by, no people

beats.say: Economists call it present bias, and it is why saving for later is hard.
beats.visual: a closed front door with a thin line of warm light underneath, no people

beats.say: The fix is not willpower. It is making the choice once, so it runs on its own.
beats.visual: a small automatic sprinkler watering a young plant at sunrise, no people

beats.say: The honest catch: it was a lab question with pretend money, mostly students, and small amounts.
beats.visual: a stormy sea with waves rising under a heavy sky and a lighthouse in the distance

beats.say: But the pattern has shown up in many studies, so plan for a brain that prefers now.
beats.visual: a single stone step leading up a long quiet staircase into morning mist, no people

beats.say: Follow for the money rules school never taught you.
beats.visual: an empty highway stretching toward a glowing sunrise horizon, wide shot

caption: In a 1981 experiment, $15 now felt as good as $100 in ten years. Present bias and how to plan for it. A lab question, not a verdict. Educational content, not financial advice.
description: In a famous 1981 experiment, people said 15 dollars today was worth the same as 100 dollars in ten years. Why the present feels so loud, and how to work with it. The honest catch: it was a hypothetical lab question.
first_comment: Which would you pick, 15 dollars now or 100 in ten years? Educational only, not financial advice.

facts.claim: Thaler (1981): median answers made people indifferent between $15 now and $20 in one month, $50 in one year, or $100 in ten years
facts.basis: Thaler 1981, Economics Letters; MIT OCW 14.13 lecture notes

facts.claim: Implied discount rates fall as the wait gets longer (hyperbolic discounting)
Catch: hypothetical questions, mostly students, small sums
